À Saint-Michel, des parents veulent comp: In Saint-Michel, Parents Want to Understand the DPJ Before Fearing It
À Saint-Michel, des parents et des jeune: In Saint-Michel, parents and young people met with the DPJ to better understand its role, dispel fears and build trust.
Kim Roiseux, Wendy Deluy et Hélène Savar: Kim Roiseux, Wendy Deluy and Hélène Savard of the DPJ, surrounded by young people and parents. Photo: Nouri N.
Le 3 juin dernier, j’ai assisté à une re: On June 3, I attended a meeting organized at the initiative of the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel between parents, young people, community workers and representatives of the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ).
À La Converse, nous nous intéressons par: At La Converse, we are particularly interested in how public institutions are perceived and experienced by immigrant, racialized and disadvantaged communities. Beyond how the DPJ works, this report seeks to understand what the questions, fears and expectations voiced by citizens reveal when they come into contact with an institution that holds such an important place in the lives of families.
La rencontre, menée sous la forme d’un q: The meeting, run as an interactive quiz, brought out the concerns, perceptions and experiences that many immigrant families in the neighbourhood associate with this institution.
Pour compléter le reportage, j’ai égalem: To round out the report, I also looked into where this initiative came from and the concerns voiced by the parents who had asked for the meeting. The subject also gave me a chance to dive into research and public documents on the criticisms levelled at the DPJ, particularly regarding Indigenous, Black and racialized communities.
<strong>Entre les parents immigrants et: Between immigrant parents and the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ), the gulf of mistrust remains hard to bridge. Even though the institution is sometimes cited as a model abroad, on the ground it still too often provokes anxiety.
<strong>À Saint-Michel, des parents ont: In Saint-Michel, parents asked to meet representatives of the institution directly so they could put their questions to them, challenge certain beliefs and better understand a system that continues to arouse mistrust.
La chaleur de ce début de juin n’a pas e: The heat of early June didn’t stop people from showing up. In the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel’s space, the seats gradually fill up. As the evening goes on, few leave before the end. For nearly two hours, parents, young people and community workers listen, ask questions and debate with representatives of the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ).
L’intérêt pour la rencontre témoigne de: The interest in the meeting reflects how important the subject is. While the DPJ is often presented as one of the pillars of Quebec’s child protection system, its name still evokes, for some families, the fear of placement, of state intervention in family life, or of consequences for their immigration journey.
Pour plusieurs parents réunis au Forum j: For several parents gathered at the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel, one question remains: how can the DPJ not be seen as an institution to be wary of?
Ce soir-là, pour briser la glace et démy: That evening, to break the ice and demystify its role, the DPJ team, made up of Wendy Deluy, Kim Roiseux and Hélène Savard, bet on an interactive quiz. Placements, immigration criteria, cultural differences: no topic was left taboo.
L’idée de cette rencontre n’est pas venu: The idea for this meeting didn’t come from the DPJ. It came from the parents themselves. “A lot of parents asked me at the beginning of the year: ‘Can we have a meeting with the DPJ?’” says Mohamed Mimoun, coordinator of the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel and the person who initiated the meeting.
Certains étaient déjà dans une situation: Some were already in a situation involving youth protection. Others simply wanted to understand. “There were a lot of situations involving their kids, mostly teens between 14 and 16,” he continues. “They had heard a lot of things about DPJ intervention: that they take the kids, that they put them in youth centres, and so on.” Through his conversations with families, he noticed that many were even hesitant to ask other services for help.
Il faut dire que l’inquiétude ambiante a: It must be said that the prevailing worry had been stirred up again a few days earlier. A video that went viral on social media showed a DPJ intervention, accompanied by police officers, with a Quebec family. Filmed by the children’s mother, the scene showed tears, screams and the distress of a family facing a placement decision.
Ne connaissant pas les détails du dossie: Not knowing the details of the case, the three DPJ representatives declined to comment on the intervention itself, which naturally came up during the discussion. They did, however, acknowledge how deeply painful such situations are, both for families and for the caseworkers called on to carry out decisions made in the best interests of children.
Pour plusieurs personnes présentes, ces: For several people present, these images feed the negative perception of the institution. For Mr. Mimoun, the best way to address that is still to let citizens put their questions directly.
Paradoxalement, les parents étaient peu: Paradoxically, few parents showed up. Only two mothers took part in the discussion, alongside several young people and community workers.
Mohamed Mimoun dit l’avoir regretté. Sel: Mohamed Mimoun said he regretted this. In his view, choosing a weeknight may have limited the participation of many parents, who are often busy with work or family responsibilities.
Celles qui étaient présentes ont toutefo: Those who were there did speak up, however. One of them questioned the anonymity of people who make a report to the DPJ. Citing situations of “revenge” and “miscommunication,” she argued that families should be able to know the identity of the person behind a report.
Les représentantes de la DPJ ont rappelé: The DPJ representatives pointed out that the confidentiality of reports is set out in law. “We’d rather have a few false reports than fail to report children who are truly in need,” replied Kim Roiseux, while acknowledging that malicious reports can sometimes happen.
Si plusieurs participants sont venus che: If many participants came looking for answers from the DPJ, it’s also because the institution carries a heavy legacy of controversy and criticism.
Au Québec, la protection de la jeunesse: In Quebec, youth protection was called deeply into question following the tragedy of <l1>the little girl from Granby</l1> in 2019. The<l2> work of the Special Commission on the Rights of Children and Youth Protection</l2>, chaired by former judge Régine Laurent, laid bare systemic failures in the flow of information, access to services and the network’s ability to meet the needs of vulnerable children.
Dans plusieurs communautés autochtones,: In several Indigenous communities, the DPJ has also been criticized for an approach seen as too removed from families’ cultural realities. Nations such as the Innu and the Atikamekw have called for greater autonomy over child protection, arguing that solutions designed by the communities themselves are often better at preserving family and cultural ties.
Dans les communautés noires, plusieurs r: In Black communities, several studies have also documented an overrepresentation of children in reports, investigations and placements. Alicia Boatswain-Kyte, assistant professor at McGill University’s School of Social Work, showed in<l1> a 2020 study</l1>, and then in a<l2> collective work</l2> published in late 2025, that a Black child is at a much higher risk of being investigated or placed than a white child.
À Saint-Michel, les questions des parent: In Saint-Michel, then, the parents’ questions go well beyond the personal: a genuine societal debate made its way into the room, particularly over how the system intervenes with families.
L’un des échanges les plus importants de: One of the most important exchanges of the evening centred on this question: “Does the DPJ often intervene in immigrant families simply because they’re immigrants, or because they have less money?”
Pour la travailleuse sociale Kim Roiseux: For social worker Kim Roiseux, the answer is no. “Cultural origin, immigration status or financial situation are not grounds for intervention,” she says. The discussion didn’t stop there, however. The caseworker acknowledges that immigrant families are more present in youth protection files. “Immigrant families are still overrepresented at the DPJ for a lot of reasons,” she explains.
Pour illustrer les situations auxquelles: To illustrate the situations she deals with, Wendy Deluy tells the story of an immigrant mother reported to the DPJ for neglect. The school was worried because the child, unlike classmates, had no meal at lunchtime. “They said it was serious neglect,” she recalls. On meeting the family, the caseworker sent by the DPJ discovered a completely different reality.
L’intervention a alors pris une autre di: The intervention then took a different direction, she continues: “We had to explain to the mother how things work here, and also explain this family’s reality to the school.”
Pour Wendy Deluy, cet exemple montre qu’: For Wendy Deluy, this example shows that a report doesn’t always correspond to a situation of abuse. “She wasn’t a neglectful mother. It was a lack of understanding of each other’s culture,” Wendy Deluy sums up, prompting approving nods in the room, where several parents fear precisely that their cultural practices will be misinterpreted.
Un autre moment fort concerne l’expressi: Another key moment concerned the expression “parental skills.” For Mohamed Mimoun, it can carry negative connotations for some immigrant families. “‘Parental skills’ is an expression that doesn’t go over well with a lot of immigrant families,” he says. “For them, being a parent is something fundamental. When you talk to them about parental skills, they may feel like you’re questioning their ability to be a father or mother.”
Plusieurs participants interviennent à l: Several participants chime in. One suggests talking about parenting strategies or tools instead. Another compares the situation to a doctor who would use only scientific jargon with patients. The DPJ representatives receive the remark with interest. “These meetings are very valuable for us,” acknowledges Hélène Savard, service head at the DPJ. “Learning that the words ‘parental skills’ can hurt some people also lets us adjust.”
Au fil de la discussion, un participant: As the discussion went on, a participant also asked whether the DPJ has adapted its practices to the evolution of Quebec society and its growing diversity.
Les représentantes de l’institution affi: The institution’s representatives say several changes have been made over the years, both in intervention approaches and in the makeup of teams. “When I started at the DPJ 26 years ago, I was the only Black woman,” says Wendy Deluy. Today, she says, caseworkers come from far more varied backgrounds. “It brings a different perspective to intervention.” She also notes that certain cultural and religious realities are now taken into account more than before, particularly when a child is placed. In her view, however, the institution still has work to do to better adapt to the diversity of the families it supports.
Parmi les questions du quiz, celle porta: Among the quiz questions, the one about immigration came up several times. For many families, the worry is real. Can a DPJ intervention jeopardize a permanent residency application? Can it affect the immigration status of parents or children?
« C’est souvent quelque chose qu’on ente: “That’s often something we hear when we get to families. People are afraid we’ll contact immigration or that it’ll leave a mark on their file,” says Kim Roiseux. And right away, she stresses that the DPJ does not contact immigration services as part of its usual interventions.
Sa collègue Wendy Deluy apporte toutefoi: Her colleague Wendy Deluy, however, adds an important nuance. She points out that situations falling under the Youth Criminal Justice Act (YCJA), which concerns young people who have committed certain criminal offences, come under a different framework than youth protection.
« Dans le cas des jeunes [qui tombent so: “In the case of young people [who fall under the YCJA], it can, and I really mean ‘can,’ have an impact on the [immigration] application. That doesn’t mean there are necessarily consequences, but the family absolutely must check with a lawyer who specializes in immigration,” she explains.
Pour les familles présentes, cette disti: For the families present, this distinction seems important. Several discover that some of the information circulating in their circles doesn’t necessarily match the reality of youth protection interventions.
Au-delà des réponses apportées aux quest: Beyond answering participants’ questions, the meeting was also meant to create a space for exchange between the institution and citizens. “Reaching out to others is super important,” says Hélène Savard, service head at the DPJ. In her view, these meetings allow parents to ask questions they might not dare to ask their own caseworker.
La démarche est également utile pour l’i: The approach is also useful for the institution itself. “If people don’t feed us input, we stay in practices that may not be the best,” she acknowledges.
Certes, une seule soirée ne balaiera pas: Admittedly, a single evening won’t sweep away decades of mistrust. But for Mohamed Mimoun, this direct dialogue is a crucial first step. To offer an alternative, Michèle Laramée, a representative of the Saint-Michel CLSC, was also on hand to present front-line support services, the ones that make it possible, precisely, to avoid reaching the point of a report.
Dans un quartier où apprivoiser le systè: In a neighbourhood where getting used to the Quebec system remains a daily challenge, the solution lies in dialogue. “Why not go get the answers at the source?” concludes Mohamed Mimoun. That evening, the parents of Saint-Michel courageously chose to ask the questions that frighten.

La travailleuse sociale évoque aussi les: The social worker also pointed to the challenges faced by newly arrived families: adapting to a new society, isolation, unfamiliarity with services, or crises tied to settling in a new country. That said, placement remains a last resort, we are told, and in the vast majority of cases, the DPJ works with the family so that the children can stay home safely. “Often, we show up, we explain things, we find the resources needed and, in the end, the DPJ doesn’t stay involved,” adds M<sup>s</sup> Roiseux.
Dans le pays d’origine de la mère, les h: In the mother’s country of origin, eating habits are different. The child was given a very hearty meal in the morning that, according to the family, covered their needs for much of the day. “When she described everything the child ate in the morning, I thought, ‘My God, that’s a whole day’s worth of food!’” says M<sup>s</sup> Deluy.
